items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Kentucky
items.storyFacts: The Lexington & Ohio began operating over its first six miles of track, animal-powered.
items.hook: It reached Frankfort in January 1834 and got its first steam locomotive in March 1836.

items.title: The president-elect's son
items.storyFacts: A Boston & Maine train derailed at Andover, Massachusetts. The only person killed was the 12-year-old son of president-elect Franklin Pierce. Pierce himself was barely hurt, but was initially reported dead  -  Congress adjourned until word came that he was safe.
items.hook: A national leadership scare and a private tragedy in the same wreck. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1853. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: The Adams Express car burglary
items.storyFacts: More than $700,000 vanished from a safe in an Adams Express car on a train running between New York and Boston. Allan Pinkerton took the case and eventually tracked the culprits down, recovering most of the money.
items.hook: Technically a burglary, not a robbery  -  nobody was present. Good hook for a segment on the difference.

items.title: Salt Lake City joins the transcontinental
items.storyFacts: The Utah Central began operating between Salt Lake City and Ogden, connecting the Mormon capital to the transcontinental line.
items.hook: Brigham Young organized it the same day the UP reached Ogden in March 1869.
items.displayName: Salt Lake City joins the transcontinental

items.title: Soldiers, a cannon, and a first
items.storyFacts: Troops and a small cannon rode the South Carolina Canal & Rail Road, one of the earliest US soldiers ever moved by train. It was an entirely peaceful trip.
items.hook: Pair with June 30, 1831  -  one of the earliest troop movement that actually saw action.
items.displayName: Soldiers, a cannon, and a first

items.title: Ground broken at Sacramento
items.storyFacts: Construction began on the Central Pacific at Sacramento.
items.hook: Six years and four months to Promontory, most of it spent on one mountain range.

items.title: Engineers and firemen strike
items.storyFacts: Engineers and firemen struck against the Michigan Southern & Northern Indiana Railroad.
items.hook: Early organized action by the operating crafts.

items.title: Erie & Kalamazoo receives a steam locomotive
items.storyFacts: The Erie & Kalamazoo receives its first steam locomotive.
items.hook: The transition from animal power to steam was underway across the young American railroad network.
items.displayName: Erie & Kalamazoo receives a steam locomotive

items.title: John Fitch is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Windsor, Connecticut. Fitch built and ran steamboats on the Delaware at Philadelphia between 1786 and 1790  -  one of the earliest steam vehicles in North America to carry paying passengers  -  and around 1798 built a working model of a steam rail car with flanged wheels.
items.hook: The steamboat pioneer who also sketched the railway. Died by opium overdose in 1798. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Panama, rails joined in the dark
items.storyFacts: The 47-and-three-quarter-mile Panama Railroad was completed when its rails were joined on a dark, stormy night. One of the earliest train ran ocean to ocean the following morning.
items.hook: One of the earliest interoceanic railway  -  and it beat the transcontinental by fourteen years.
items.displayName: Panama, rails joined in the dark

items.title: Asa Whitney asks Congress for a Pacific railroad
items.storyFacts: The New York merchant proposed a railroad to the Pacific, funded partly by federal land grant. Whitney had wealth and influence enough to be taken seriously.
items.hook: The idea arrives 24 years before the Golden Spike. Whitney's rival John Plumbe later published a pamphlet attacking the scheme.
items.displayName: Asa Whitney asks Congress for a Pacific railroad

items.title: First Panama Railroad train crosses the isthmus
items.storyFacts: A train runs from the Atlantic to the Pacific across the completed Panama Railroad, one day after the last rail was joined.
items.hook: The 47-mile route cut a major ocean-to-ocean journey to a matter of hours.
items.displayName: First Panama Railroad train crosses the isthmus

items.title: First railroad in North Carolina
items.storyFacts: The Wilmington & Weldon opened. By 1840 it ran 161 miles between Wilmington and Weldon on the Roanoke River.
items.hook: It was chartered as the Wilmington & Raleigh. It never went to Raleigh.

items.title: Washington can seize the railroads
items.storyFacts: Congress passed the Railways and Telegraph Act, authorizing the federal government to take control of any railroad property deemed necessary for public safety. Seized property went into the US Military Railroad.
items.hook: One of the earliest time Washington claimed the power to nationalize a railroad. It did so again in 1917.

items.title: Oxen on the Southern Pacific
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest train of three cars was hauled by oxen between Swanson's Landing and Marshall, Texas on the Southern Pacific Railroad Co. of Texas.
items.hook: The Southern Pacific began behind oxen.

items.title: The Michigan Central opens
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest 30 miles of the state-owned Michigan Central opened between Detroit and Ypsilanti.
items.hook: Michigan built it, went broke, and sold it in 1846.

items.title: Edison's train newspaper
items.storyFacts: Thomas Edison printed and sold one of the earliest issue of his Grand Trunk Herald aboard a train running between Port Huron and Detroit.
items.hook: A teenage news butch running a printing press in a baggage car.

items.title: The patent behind 25,000 locomotives
items.storyFacts: Henry R. Campbell, chief engineer of the Philadelphia, Germantown & Norristown, patented a locomotive with a swiveling truck  -  one of the earliest 4-4-0 arrangement.
items.hook: More than 25,000 were eventually built in the US, the most numerous type in the country's history.

items.title: The first US railroad charter
items.storyFacts: New Jersey chartered a company to build a rail road from the Delaware near Trenton to the Raritan at New Brunswick, as proposed by John Stevens. It was the first railroad charter issued in the United States.
items.hook: Nothing was built for years. The charter came first, the railroad much later.

items.title: Thomas Edison is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Milan, Ohio.
items.hook: He got his start selling newspapers on the Grand Trunk and printing his own aboard the train.

items.title: Lincoln leaves Springfield
items.storyFacts: A special train left Springfield, Illinois carrying president-elect Abraham Lincoln and his family to Washington.
items.hook: He told the crowd he did not know whether he would ever return. He returned in 1865, on a train.

items.title: The first railroad in Vermont
items.storyFacts: The Vermont Central opened for business between Burlington and Windsor.
items.hook: Chartered in 1843, six years to build across the Green Mountains.

items.title: The Hannibal & St. Joseph opens end to end
items.storyFacts: The line began operating over its entire route between the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers.
items.hook: A year later it would carry the Pony Express mail, and in 1862 pioneer the sorting of mail in motion.
items.displayName: The Hannibal & St. Joseph opens end to end

items.title: Crossing the Hudson at Albany
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest train crossed the Hudson River bridge at Albany; one of the earliest passenger train followed on February 22. The bridge was owned by a company half held by the New York Central.
items.hook: Within a year Vanderbilt would use his control of the other side to strangle the Central into selling.

items.title: Pullman absorbs his rival
items.storyFacts: Pullman's Palace Car Company leased the Central Transportation Company, which held the assets and patents of Andrew Carnegie and Theodore T. Woodruff.
items.hook: Woodruff patented the sleeping car berth in 1856. Pullman ended up owning the market.

items.title: First to the Mississippi
items.storyFacts: The Chicago & Rock Island entered Rock Island, Illinois  -  one of the earliest railroad to reach the Mississippi River from the east.
items.hook: Two years later its bridge over that river would put Abraham Lincoln in a courtroom.

items.title: First railroad in California
items.storyFacts: The Sacramento Valley Railroad was completed between Sacramento and Folsom.
items.hook: Gold Rush infrastructure. Theodore Judah engineered it before turning to the transcontinental.

items.title: Lincoln slips through Baltimore
items.storyFacts: Warned of an assassination plot, the president-elect left his family in Harrisburg and departed after dark on a special train, with every telegraph line out of the city cut. Not expected in Baltimore until afternoon, his train passed through without incident.
items.hook: The most consequential night ride in American railroad history.

items.title: Milwaukee's first line
items.storyFacts: The Milwaukee & Mississippi began service between Milwaukee and Waukesha, Wisconsin.
items.hook: The beginning of the Milwaukee Road.

items.title: The Baltimore & Ohio is chartered
items.storyFacts: An act of the Maryland legislature chartered the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad.
items.hook: America's first common-carrier railroad begins as a piece of paper. Construction started July 4, 1828.

items.title: A locomotive on a postage stamp
items.storyFacts: US postage stamps issued this day included a three-cent blue depicting a locomotive, designed by the National Bank Note Company of New York.
items.hook: The railroad had become national iconography within forty years.
items.displayName: A locomotive on a postage stamp

items.title: George Pullman is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Brocton, Chautauqua County, New York.
items.hook: His name became a byword for luxury travel, a company town, and one of the bitterest strikes in US history.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad land grant
items.storyFacts: Congress granted right-of-way through public lands plus additional privileges to Florida's Tallahassee Railroad Company  -  one of the earliest public land grant to a railroad. Similar grants had previously gone to roads and canals.
items.hook: The template for the vast land grants that built the West.

items.title: Theodore Judah is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Bridgeport, Connecticut.
items.hook: Crazy Judah, they called him. He surveyed the route over the Sierra Nevada that everyone said was impossible.

items.title: Harnden begins rail-and-steam express service
items.storyFacts: William Frederick Harnden begins an express service between New York and Boston using rail and steamship connections.
items.hook: Express companies grew alongside railroads because trains created reliable long-distance schedules.

items.title: Utah Central is organized
items.storyFacts: Union Pacific reaches Ogden, and Brigham Young and other Mormon leaders organize the Utah Central Railroad to build toward Salt Lake City.
items.hook: The new line would connect Utah's capital directly to the transcontinental railroad.

items.title: The Desjardins Canal disaster
items.storyFacts: A Great Western passenger train derailed crossing a bridge near Hamilton, Ontario, collapsing the structure into the frozen canal below. Sixty of the ninety people aboard died.
items.hook: A defining Canadian disaster and an early argument for bridge inspection. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad tunnel in the United States
items.storyFacts: The 901-foot Staple Bend Tunnel near Johnstown, Pennsylvania, was completed on the Allegheny Portage Railroad. The same date marked completion of one of the earliest track of the 36.7-mile line linking canals at Hollidaysburg and Johnstown.
items.hook: It still stands. The Allegheny Portage hauled canal boats over a mountain on inclined planes.
items.displayName: The first railroad tunnel in the United States

items.title: Wells and Fargo walk out
items.storyFacts: Henry Wells and William Fargo left American Express to establish Wells, Fargo & Company after American Express vetoed their proposal to compete in the booming California trade.
items.hook: A rejected business plan that became a household name.

items.title: Rudolf Diesel is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Paris.
items.hook: The engine bearing his name would end the steam era. He vanished from a Channel steamer in 1913.
sources: Britannica and Encyclopedia.com, cross-checked 2026-08-30: 18 March 1858, 38 Rue Notre-Dame-de-Nazareth, Paris

items.title: One of the earliest ten-wheeler
items.storyFacts: The 4-6-0 Chesapeake arrived on the Philadelphia & Reading with its builder Septimus Norris. On almost the same day Hinkley & Drury of Boston delivered the 4-6-0 New Hampshire to the Boston & Maine.
items.hook: Credit for the design is genuinely uncertain  -  two builders, one week. Over 17,000 were eventually built.

items.title: Michigan authorizes sale of state railroads
items.storyFacts: Michigan legislators authorize the sale of the state-owned Michigan Central, part of a broader shift toward private railroad ownership.
items.hook: Railroad financing and ownership were changing as networks expanded.
items.displayName: Michigan authorizes sale of state railroads

items.title: Miller's coupler
items.storyFacts: Ezra Miller received a patent for an improved hook-type coupler. A January 1865 improvement added a passenger car end platform and buffer; by 1875 the Miller system was used by 85 percent of North American railroads.
items.hook: The link-and-pin coupler it replaced cost brakemen their fingers, hands, and lives.

items.title: The inclined plane cable snaps
items.storyFacts: Three died in an accident caused by a broken cable on an inclined plane of the Lexington & Ohio at Frankfort, Kentucky.
items.hook: Inclined planes were how early railroads crossed hills. When the cable went, nothing stopped the car. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: The steepest grade in America
items.storyFacts: The Madison & Lafayette opened between Madison and Vernon, Indiana. The climb up from the Ohio River at Madison runs at 5.89 percent  -  steepest then known railroad grade in the United States. The section was worked with rack assistance.
items.hook: Nearly six percent. Most main lines never exceed two.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1839. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Railway Age publishes its first issue
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest issue of Railway Age magazine appeared.
items.hook: Still publishing today  -  one of the sources feeding this very show.
items.displayName: Railway Age publishes its first issue

items.title: Pony Express begins
items.storyFacts: Overland mail service to California begins as one of the earliest Pony Express rider departs St. Joseph, Missouri.
items.hook: The Pony Express was a relay of riders and horses - not a train - but it depended on railroad connections at the eastern end.

items.title: Western Union is chartered
items.storyFacts: The Western Union Telegraph Company is chartered by New York State.
items.hook: Railroads and telegraphs developed together, allowing train movements and business information to travel faster.

items.title: The Granger laws begin
items.storyFacts: Illinois established a state railroad and warehouse commission, believed to be one of the earliest Granger legislation enacted by a state.
items.hook: Farmers organizing against freight rates  -  the beginning of railroad regulation in America.

items.title: The Erie is completed
items.storyFacts: The last spike was driven at Cuba, New York, completing the Erie Railroad between the Hudson at Pierpont and Lake Erie at Dunkirk.
items.hook: Six-foot gauge, and for a while longest then known railroad in the world.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1851. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Grenville Dodge is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Danvers, Massachusetts.
items.hook: Chief engineer of the Union Pacific. He met Lincoln in Council Bluffs in 1859 and convinced him a Pacific railroad was feasible.

items.title: The Pennsylvania Railroad is chartered
items.storyFacts: The state charter required the railroad to pay a tonnage tax, protecting state canal revenue.
items.hook: The Standard Railroad of the World starts out taxed to protect a canal.

items.title: Crozet's tunnel opens
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest train ran through the Blue Ridge (Crozet) Tunnel near Waynesboro, Virginia, designed and built by French civil engineer Claudius Crozet. At 4,273 feet it was longest then known railroad tunnel in the world.
items.hook: Bored largely by hand and by Irish immigrant labor, through solid rock, without power tools.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1858. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Westinghouse patents the air brake
items.storyFacts: Twenty-two-year-old George Westinghouse received a patent for his straight-air brake. The Westinghouse Air Brake Company was incorporated that September.
items.hook: Arguably the most important safety invention in railroad history  -  and he was 22.

items.title: Sabotage at Carr's Rock
items.storyFacts: An Erie express derailed along the Delaware River near Port Jervis, New York, killing 24. A disgruntled former railroad employee was arrested for sabotage. John Bowen later pleaded guilty and received a ten-year sentence.
items.hook: An early case of deliberate train wrecking, with a conviction. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Columbia River Portage Railroad opens
items.storyFacts: The Columbia River Portage Railroad opens to bypass rapids between The Dalles and Celilo in Oregon.
items.hook: Railroads could solve navigation problems that water transport could not.

items.title: The funeral train departs
items.storyFacts: Abraham Lincoln's funeral train left Washington, scheduled to stop for tributes in virtually every major city of the North.
items.hook: A 1,600-mile procession watched by millions standing at the lineside.

items.title: The bridge that changed everything
items.storyFacts: The Chicago & Rock Island's 1,535-foot bridge across the Mississippi was completed, connecting Rock Island, Illinois with Davenport, Iowa.
items.hook: Two weeks later a steamboat hit it, and the resulting lawsuit made Lincoln a railroad lawyer.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Louisiana
items.storyFacts: The Pontchartrain Railroad began operating between the Mississippi River and Lake Pontchartrain at New Orleans, animal-powered. A British locomotive named Pontchartrain took over in September 1832.
items.hook: One of the oldest railroads in the United States, and it ran on mule power first.

items.title: Michigan Central reaches Lake Michigan
items.storyFacts: The Michigan Central reaches Lake Michigan at New Buffalo.
items.hook: A rail connection to the lake strengthened Detroit's position in the growing Great Lakes network.

items.title: A model locomotive begins operation
items.storyFacts: A model locomotive capable of hauling two small passenger cars begins operation in the United States.
items.hook: Early American engineers were testing locomotive designs on a tiny scale.

items.title: Grand Crossing
items.storyFacts: A Michigan Southern express rammed a Michigan Central passenger train carrying mostly German immigrants south of Chicago. Twenty-one died. Before this, no single US railroad accident had killed more than seven.
items.hook: The moment American railroading crossed a threshold in scale of harm. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Ten miles of track in one day
items.storyFacts: Central Pacific crews laid ten miles of track in a single twelve-hour day in Utah. The stunt took more than a week to prepare and settled a $10,000 wager between the CP's Charles Crocker and the UP's Thomas Durant. Crocker won.
items.hook: A record that stood  -  and a bet that paid.
items.displayName: Ten miles of track in one day

items.title: New York restricts railroad competition with canals
items.storyFacts: New York grants the Utica & Schenectady Railroad a charter restricting the freight it may carry, part of a broader effort to protect the Erie Canal.
items.hook: Railroads were initially treated as competitors to established canal monopolies.
items.displayName: New York restricts railroad competition with canals

items.title: A battery-electric railcar in 1851
items.storyFacts: Dr. Charles G. Page of the US Patent Office tested a 16-horsepower battery-powered electric rail car over the B&O between Washington and Bladensburg, Maryland, built on a four-wheel flat car the railroad supplied.
items.hook: Battery electric traction, eighteen years before the Golden Spike.

items.title: Lincoln comes home
items.storyFacts: Abraham Lincoln's body returned to Springfield, Illinois over the Chicago & Alton, traveling in George Pullman's experimental sleeping car Pioneer.
items.hook: The funeral train made Pullman's name. The car had to be accommodated at stations along the route.

items.title: The Norwalk drawbridge
items.storyFacts: An eastbound New York & New Haven train ran past a signal indicating an open drawbridge and plunged into the Norwalk River at South Norwalk, Connecticut. Forty-six died.
items.hook: The second major American rail disaster in under two weeks  -  see April 25, 1853. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: The Effie Afton hits the bridge
items.storyFacts: The steamboat Effie Afton collided with the new Rock Island bridge, starting a fire that destroyed the boat and part of the structure. The railroad was promptly sued, and it was widely believed steamboat interests had encouraged the collision to test whether railroads could bridge navigable rivers.
items.hook: Abraham Lincoln defended the railroad. Rail versus river, argued in court.
items.displayName: The Effie Afton hits the bridge

items.title: One of the earliest 4-4-0 is built
items.storyFacts: James Brooks constructed one of the earliest 4-4-0 locomotive to Henry Campbell's design in the Philadelphia suburb of Frankford.
items.hook: The American Standard. It would define the look of a locomotive for fifty years.

items.title: The Oregon Pony
items.storyFacts: The locomotive Oregon Pony began steam operation on the Oregon Portage Railway along the Columbia River, offering a short ride between steamboats that could not pass the Cascade rapids.
items.hook: A railroad that existed purely to get around a rapid.

items.title: The Golden Spike
items.storyFacts: Central Pacific and Union Pacific rails were formally joined at Promontory, Utah, a desolate spot north of the Great Salt Lake, completing the Pacific railroad Congress had authorized seven years earlier. By prior negotiation the two companies actually connected at Ogden.
items.hook: The ceremony and the operational junction were in different places  -  a good myth-correction beat.

items.title: Daniel Webster in a rocking chair
items.storyFacts: Special trains on the Erie carried President Fillmore, New York governor William Seward and Senator Stephen Douglas. Secretary of State Daniel Webster took in the scenery from a rocking chair secured to a flatcar.
items.hook: The Secretary of State rode an open flatcar in a rocking chair. Nobody stopped him.
items.displayName: Daniel Webster in a rocking chair

items.title: Regular transcontinental service
items.storyFacts: Regular service began on the transcontinental railroad between Omaha and Sacramento, five days after the Promontory ceremony.
items.hook: True Atlantic-to-Pacific rail travel still needed years of connecting bridges. The Missouri at Omaha was crossed by ferry until 1872.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad strike
items.storyFacts: The Public Ledger reported what appears to be one of the earliest organized work stoppage against a US railroad: laborers at Bordentown, New Jersey struck to protest an increase in working hours.
items.hook: American railroad labor organizing begins in year one of the industry.

items.title: The Homestead Act
items.storyFacts: Lincoln signed the act granting 160 acres to any citizen or immigrant willing to occupy and farm the land for five years.
items.hook: Land settlement and railroad land grants were two halves of the same westward machine.

items.title: One of the earliest paying passengers in North America
items.storyFacts: Fifteen miles of the Baltimore & Ohio opened for regular service from Pratt Street in Baltimore to Ellicott's Mills. The railroad contracted a stagecoach operator for drivers and horses, changing teams at Relay House.
items.hook: One of the earliest North American railroad to carry revenue passengers  -  and it was horse-drawn.
items.displayName: The first paying passengers in North America

items.title: What hath God wrought, along the B&O
items.storyFacts: Samuel Morse transmitted a telegraphic message from the Capitol in Washington to the Baltimore & Ohio depot in Baltimore. One of the earliest US telegraph line ran on wooden poles along the B&O right-of-way.
items.hook: The Baltimore end is often wrongly given as Mt. Clare, then a minor stop. The main depot was on Pratt Street.
items.displayName: What hath God wrought, along the B&O

items.title: One of the earliest American steel rails
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest steel rails rolled in the US were produced at Chicago Rolling Mills from ingots made at the Eureka Iron Works in Wyandotte, Michigan. They weighed 57 pounds to the yard. The Chicago & North Western was one of the earliest buyer.
items.hook: Iron rails wore out in months under traffic. Steel changed the economics of the whole industry.

items.title: John Plumbe's end
items.storyFacts: John Plumbe Jr., a longtime promoter of a northern transcontinental railroad, took his own life at his brother's home in Dubuque, Iowa. His daguerreotype business had failed and he had been ill with recurring malaria contracted in California.
items.hook: A visionary who died broke while the idea he championed went to others. Handle with care on air. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Water at speed
items.storyFacts: Track pans went into service on the New York Central & Hudson River Railroad at Montrose, New York, one of the earliest in the US. The shallow troughs between the rails let locomotives scoop up water without stopping.
items.hook: Refuelling at 50 mph, using nothing but a scoop and momentum.

items.title: Mules up, gravity down
items.storyFacts: The Summit Hill-Mauch Chunk Railroad opened, connecting a coal mine at Summit Hill, Pennsylvania with the Lehigh River. Mules hauled empty cars uphill; loaded cars returned by gravity, along with a car for the mules.
items.hook: It later became a tourist ride  -  arguably America's first roller coaster.

items.title: One of the earliest sitting president to ride a train
items.storyFacts: Andrew Jackson rode the Baltimore & Ohio from Ellicott City to Baltimore.
items.hook: John Quincy Adams had ridden in 1830  -  but out of office. Jackson was one of the earliest while serving.
items.displayName: The first sitting president to ride a train

items.title: Denver gets its connection
items.storyFacts: The Denver Pacific Railroad opened, connecting Denver with the Union Pacific at Cheyenne, Wyoming.
items.hook: Denver had been bypassed by the transcontinental. The city built its own link rather than accept it.

items.title: Pennsylvania Railroad bids for state Main Line
items.storyFacts: The Pennsylvania Railroad becomes the only bidder for Pennsylvania's state-owned Main Line of Public Works.
items.hook: The deal helped turn a mixed canal-and-rail system into a privately controlled railroad corridor.
items.displayName: Pennsylvania Railroad bids for state Main Line
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1857. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: The Boston & Lowell opens
items.storyFacts: The line opened between its two namesake cities in Massachusetts.
items.hook: Built to serve the textile mills  -  industrial railroading from day one.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Rhode Island
items.storyFacts: The entire 43.5 miles of the Boston & Providence was completed. Passengers heading to New York could connect at Providence with Cornelius Vanderbilt's new steamboat Lexington.
items.hook: Rail plus steamboat was the fast route between Boston and New York for years.
items.displayName: The first railroad in Rhode Island

items.title: St-Hilaire
items.storyFacts: An immigrant train from Quebec ran through an open drawbridge over the Richelieu River at St-Hilaire. The exact toll aboard the Grand Trunk train is unknown  -  sources give between 86 and 100 dead. It remains the worst rail disaster in North America.
items.hook: The death toll is still uncertain, because nobody knew exactly who was aboard an immigrant train. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Troops by rail, into action
items.storyFacts: About 100 members of Maryland's Light Brigade militia rode the Baltimore & Ohio to quell a riot among railroad workers at Sykes's Mill. They were one of the earliest US troops moved by rail to see action  -  though they had to march the last seven miles from the end of track.
items.hook: One of the earliest military rail deployment in America was against railroad workers.

items.title: Insuring the boiler
items.storyFacts: The Hartford Steam Boiler Inspection & Insurance Company was incorporated in Connecticut. Its founders were spurred by the April 1865 boiler explosion aboard the steamboat Sultana, which killed over 1,600.
items.hook: Steam power created a whole insurance industry because it kept killing people. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: B&O's Washington branch is toured
items.storyFacts: Baltimore & Ohio officers and guests tour the newly completed branch to Washington.
items.hook: The branch linked Baltimore's railroad network with the national capital.

items.title: Refrigerated freight car carries butter
items.storyFacts: A Northern Railroad boxcar modified for ice is used to ship eight tons of butter to Boston.
items.hook: Refrigeration by rail helped transform food distribution over long distances.

items.title: Lincoln signs the Pacific Railroad Act
items.storyFacts: The act incorporated the Union Pacific to build west from the Missouri River and authorized the Central Pacific to build east from Sacramento, with a telegraph line along the route. Track gauge was left undetermined.
items.hook: They authorized a transcontinental railroad without deciding how wide it would be. Congress set 4 ft 8.5 in the following March.
items.displayName: Lincoln signs the Pacific Railroad Act

items.title: Confederation, on the promise of railroads
items.storyFacts: The British North America Act created the Dominion of Canada. As a condition of confederation, the Dominion government agreed to take control of existing railroads in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and extend them to connect with lines in Quebec.
items.hook: Canada was assembled with railway promises. British Columbia joined in 1871 on the same terms.
items.displayName: Confederation, on the promise of railroads

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Minnesota
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest ten miles of the St. Paul & Pacific opened between St. Paul and St. Anthony, now Minneapolis.
items.hook: This ten-mile stub eventually became James J. Hill's Great Northern.

items.title: To the top of Mount Washington
items.storyFacts: The Mount Washington Cog Railway was completed, climbing three and a half miles to a 6,288-foot summit in New Hampshire.
items.hook: The world's first mountain-climbing cog railway. It is still running.
items.displayName: To the top of Mount Washington

items.title: One of the earliest bridge across the Missouri
items.storyFacts: The 1,400-foot Hannibal Bridge at Kansas City opened, one of the earliest railroad bridge over the Missouri River, designed by French-born engineer Octave Chanute.
items.hook: Chanute later became a pioneer of aviation and corresponded with the Wright brothers.
items.displayName: The first bridge across the Missouri

items.title: Charles Carroll turns one of the earliest spade
items.storyFacts: Ceremonies in Baltimore marked the start of work on the Baltimore & Ohio. Charles Carroll, the last surviving signer of the Declaration of Independence and a B&O director, presided.
items.hook: The last living signer of the Declaration launched the American railroad age, on Independence Day.
items.displayName: Charles Carroll turns the first spade

items.title: First railroad in Delaware
items.storyFacts: The New Castle & Frenchtown Railroad opened, spanning 17 miles between Frenchtown, Maryland and New Castle, Delaware.
items.hook: A rail portage between two navigable waters  -  the classic early American railroad job.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Indiana
items.storyFacts: The 1.25-mile Lawrenceburgh & Indianapolis carried holiday crowds in its single horse-drawn car.
items.hook: A mile and a quarter, one car, one horse, and a name that promised a whole state.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Ohio
items.storyFacts: Passenger service began on the Cleveland & Newburgh Railway along Euclid Avenue between 101st Street and Public Square. Built mainly to haul stone and lumber, it was animal-powered.
items.hook: Ohio's first railroad was effectively a street tramway.

items.title: Every railroad becomes a post road
items.storyFacts: President Van Buren signed a bill designating all railroads as postal routes.
items.hook: One signature turned the entire rail network into mail infrastructure.
items.displayName: Every railroad becomes a post road

items.title: Union Pacific begins track-laying west from Omaha
items.storyFacts: Track-laying begins on the Union Pacific west from Omaha, Nebraska.
items.hook: This was the physical start of the Union Pacific's push toward the transcontinental connection.
items.displayName: Union Pacific begins track-laying west from Omaha

items.title: US Patent No. 1
items.storyFacts: Patent number one under the restarted numbering system was issued to John Ruggles for an improvement to railroad locomotives.
items.hook: The very first numbered US patent is a railroad patent. The almanac itself flags this one with a query  -  verify before airing.

items.title: The Grand Trunk is formed
items.storyFacts: Six Canadian railroads combined to form the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
items.hook: It became the backbone of Canadian railroading and eventually part of Canadian National.

items.title: Shohola
items.storyFacts: An Erie train carrying Confederate prisoners of war collided head-on with a coal train near Shohola, New York. Roughly 60 died, including 17 Union guards.
items.hook: Prisoners and their guards killed together, and buried together. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Pullman's Palace Car Company
items.storyFacts: Pullman's Palace Car Company was incorporated.
items.hook: It would become largest then known employer of Black Americans in the country, and the cradle of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1867. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Camp Hill
items.storyFacts: An excursion train of the North Pennsylvania Railroad carrying Philadelphia schoolchildren to a country outing collided head-on with a regular train. At least sixty died, all of them on the special, which caught fire on impact.
items.hook: A children's day out. It drove major reform in how trains were dispatched. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Portland-Montreal international rail route completed
items.storyFacts: An international rail route connecting Portland, Maine, with Montreal is completed.
items.hook: Railroads were beginning to link national networks across international borders.

items.title: British Columbia joins for a railway
items.storyFacts: British Columbia entered the Dominion of Canada on the promise that the national government would begin building a railroad linking the province to the rest of the country within two years, and finish within ten.
items.hook: A province bought with a railway. The CPR took fourteen years.
items.displayName: British Columbia joins for a railway

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Canada
items.storyFacts: The Champlain & St. Lawrence opened between St. John's and the St. Lawrence near LaPrairie, Lower Canada.
items.hook: The almanac notes a disputed circa-1826 claim near Kingsley, Quebec  -  a good 'what counts as first' segment.

items.title: Frank Sprague is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Milford, Connecticut.
items.hook: The father of electric traction  -  his Richmond streetcar system in 1888 set the pattern for electric railways worldwide.

items.title: Sorting the mail in motion
items.storyFacts: William A. Davis, assistant postmaster at St. Joseph, Missouri, began sorting California-bound mail aboard the Hannibal & St. Joseph using a modified baggage car. This led directly to the purpose-built Railway Post Office.
items.hook: The idea was to sort while moving so the mail was ready the instant it arrived.

items.title: An American builds the Czar's railway
items.storyFacts: George Washington Whistler arrived in St. Petersburg to begin construction of a railroad from St. Petersburg to Moscow.
items.hook: He died of cholera there in 1849. His son was the painter James McNeill Whistler. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.
items.displayName: An American builds the Czar's railway

items.title: First railroad in Texas
items.storyFacts: Service began on one of the earliest 20 miles of the Buffalo Bayou, Brazos & Colorado, running west from Harrisburg near Houston.
items.hook: Texas came late to rail and then built more of it than any other state.

items.title: Grand Trunk leases Atlantic & St. Lawrence
items.storyFacts: The Grand Trunk Railway leases the Atlantic & St. Lawrence Railroad.
items.hook: Leasing and consolidation were early tools for creating long-distance systems.
items.displayName: Grand Trunk leases Atlantic & St. Lawrence

items.title: The Lion at Honesdale
items.storyFacts: A locomotive built in Stourbridge, England and driven by engineer Horatio Allen was tested on the Delaware & Hudson Canal Company's railroad in Pennsylvania. Judged too heavy for the Lackawaxen River bridge, the eight-ton import was taken off the rails and abandoned. It was still one of the earliest steam locomotive to run on a commercial railroad in North America.
items.hook: Commonly called the Stourbridge Lion  -  but a contemporary newspaper account of its arrival says it was simply The Lion. Its front carried a fierce lion's face.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1829. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Cuba's railroad commission meets
items.storyFacts: The governor of Cuba presides over one of the earliest meeting of the Junta de Caminos de Hierro, the island's railroad commission.
items.hook: Cuba was moving toward one of the earliest railways outside Europe and North America.

items.title: The DeWitt Clinton runs to Schenectady
items.storyFacts: The locomotive DeWitt Clinton hauled a train from Albany to Schenectady over the Mohawk & Hudson, one of the earliest railroad in New York.
items.hook: Artist William H. Brown sketched the train before boarding, producing the famous silhouette.
items.displayName: The DeWitt Clinton runs to Schenectady

items.title: CB&Q opens Mississippi River bridge at Burlington
items.storyFacts: The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy opens its 2,237-foot iron bridge across the Mississippi at Burlington, Iowa.
items.hook: Major river bridges eliminated ferries and made through rail routes possible.
items.displayName: CB&Q opens Mississippi River bridge at Burlington

items.title: Pullman's first sleeping car
items.storyFacts: George Pullman and partner Benjamin Field demonstrated their first sleeping car in Chicago.
items.hook: Sleeping cars already existed since 1838. Pullman's contribution was standardization, luxury, and a business model.

items.title: The Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers
items.storyFacts: At a national meeting in Indianapolis, the Brotherhood of the Foot Board changed its name to the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers.
items.hook: Founded in Detroit in May 1863 by thirteen Michigan Central engineers meeting in a private house.

items.title: Imperial Mexican Railway Company is formed
items.storyFacts: Don Antonio Escandon and British investors form the Imperial Mexican Railway Company to build a railroad between Mexico City and Veracruz.
items.hook: Railway finance in Mexico drew international capital during a turbulent political era.
items.displayName: Imperial Mexican Railway Company is formed

items.title: Eastern Railroad opens Boston-Salem
items.storyFacts: The Eastern Railroad opens for traffic between Boston and Salem, Massachusetts.
items.hook: Short intercity corridors were becoming the backbone of New England's early rail network.

items.title: Peter Cooper's little engine
items.storyFacts: Cooper's locomotive pulled a regular train on a round trip over the Baltimore & Ohio, making the return in record time and becoming one of the earliest American-built locomotive to carry revenue passengers.
items.hook: It was almost certainly never called Tom Thumb in its lifetime. The name comes from an 1868 speech by John H.B. Latrobe, borrowing the stage name of the era's most famous performer.

items.title: One of the earliest Railway Post Office car
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest car built specifically as a US Railway Post Office entered service between Chicago and Clinton, Iowa on the Chicago & North Western.
items.hook: Mail sorted at speed, in a moving room. The RPO ran for over a century.
items.displayName: The first Railway Post Office car

items.title: Lincoln inspects a burned bridge
items.storyFacts: Hired to defend the railroad in the Rock Island bridge case, Abraham Lincoln visited the ruined structure to interview witnesses and gather evidence.
items.hook: Lincoln on site, walking the wreckage. He won.

items.title: Atlanta's ammunition trains
items.storyFacts: Confederate forces evacuating Atlanta and unable to move 81 boxcars of ammunition detonated the explosives rather than leave them to the approaching Union army.
items.hook: Eighty-one boxcars. The explosion is the one staged in Gone with the Wind.

items.title: One of the earliest cattle train from Abilene
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest trainload of longhorn cattle left Abilene, Kansas for Chicago, beginning the era of overland drives from central Texas to railheads along the Kansas Pacific. By the end of 1869, an estimated 150,000 longhorns a year were being shipped out of Abilene.
items.hook: The cattle drive existed to reach a railroad. The cowboy is a rail story.
items.displayName: The first cattle train from Abilene

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Arkansas
items.storyFacts: Prominent citizens and press rode a special train over the Memphis & Little Rock from Hopefield, Arkansas to the end of track about ten miles west.
items.hook: The line was not completed to Little Rock until April 1871  -  fifteen years later.

items.title: Western Railroad opens Boston-Albany
items.storyFacts: Service begins between Boston and Albany over the Western Railroad.
items.hook: The line helped connect New England's largest then known city with the Hudson Valley and western markets.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1842. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: The Oruktor Amphibolos
items.storyFacts: Oliver Evans's steam-powered dredge travelled under its own power from his Philadelphia shop up Market Street and around Centre Square to the Schuylkill River. Fitted with temporary wheels and drive pulleys, it was one of the earliest self-propelled land vehicle in North America.
items.hook: An amphibious steam dredge, driving itself through downtown Philadelphia in 1804.

items.title: James J. Hill is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Rockwood, Ontario.
items.hook: The Empire Builder  -  he built the Great Northern to the Pacific without a single federal land grant.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Mexico
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest section of the Vera Cruz-Rio San Juan Railway was ceremonially opened. Regular service between Veracruz and El Molino began on September 22.
items.hook: Note the two dates  -  ceremonial versus regular service. A recurring trap in rail chronology.

items.title: Juarez opens the Mexican Railway
items.storyFacts: President Benito Juarez officially opened a section of the Mexican Railway between Mexico City and Puebla.
items.hook: Mexico's trunk railway was built by a company that had been the Imperial Mexican Railway until Maximilian fell.

items.title: Standardizing the freight car
items.storyFacts: Delegates from at least 29 railroads met in Altoona, Pennsylvania to form the Master Car Builders Association.
items.hook: Interchange only works if everyone's cars match. This is where that got decided.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1867. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Pacific Railroad reaches Kansas City
items.storyFacts: A final spike completes the Pacific Railroad between St. Louis and Kansas City.
items.hook: The Missouri rail network was being tied into a broader national system.

items.title: The Central Railroad Act
items.storyFacts: President Fillmore signed a land-grant bill aiding railroad construction, initially benefiting the Illinois Central and Mobile & Ohio, intended to create a Great Lakes-to-Gulf railroad.
items.hook: The land grant model that would later build the transcontinentals.

items.title: One of the earliest orphan train
items.storyFacts: The Children's Aid Society sent a group of homeless children by boat and train from New York City to Dowagiac, Michigan, for placement in permanent homes. It was one of the earliest of the orphan trains.
items.hook: Over seventy years, roughly a quarter of a million children were moved this way.

items.title: One of the earliest train order by telegraph
items.storyFacts: Erie superintendent Charles Minot, waiting impatiently at a station for an opposing train, used the commercial telegraph to order that train held at the next station  -  one of the earliest known use of telegraphy to regulate train movements.
items.hook: His engineer reportedly refused to move, so Minot drove the locomotive himself. The single most important operating innovation in railroad history.
items.displayName: The first train order by telegraph

items.title: The pop valve
items.storyFacts: George W. Richardson patented an improved automatic safety valve, known as the pop valve for its quick-opening action.
items.hook: That distinctive hiss-and-bang of a steam locomotive at rest is Richardson's patent.

items.title: One of the earliest union station
items.storyFacts: The Union Track Railway's passenger depot opened at Indianapolis, one of the earliest union station in the United States.
items.hook: One building, several competing railroads  -  a genuinely new idea in 1853.

items.title: Madison & Indianapolis opens to the Ohio River
items.storyFacts: The Madison & Indianapolis opens for traffic between Indiana's capital and the Ohio River.
items.hook: The route connected Indianapolis with a major river gateway.
items.displayName: Madison & Indianapolis opens to the Ohio River

items.title: One of the earliest interlocking in America
items.storyFacts: The United New Jersey Railroad & Canal Company installed a British-made Saxby & Farmer interlocking frame at Top-of-the-Hill near Trenton, one of the earliest in the US.
items.hook: Rows of huge levers, hundreds of feet of rodding, and enough friction that the operators were called armstrong men.

items.title: The longest railroad in the world
items.storyFacts: The South Carolina Canal & Rail Road completed its line from Charleston to Hamburg on the Savannah River. At 136 miles it was longest then known railroad in the world.
items.hook: The record moved to the B&O the following year at 137 miles. Records were measured in single miles then.
items.displayName: The longest railroad in the world
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1833. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Morse patents the telegraph
items.storyFacts: Samuel Morse received a US patent for his electric telegraph.
items.hook: Within fifteen years it would be running railroads, not just messages.

items.title: First railroad bridge over the Hudson
items.storyFacts: The Rensselaer & Saratoga completed one of the earliest railroad bridge across the Hudson River at Troy, New York.
items.hook: The Hudson was the great barrier for New York railroading. Manhattan itself waited until 1910 for a tunnel.
items.displayName: First railroad bridge over the Hudson

items.title: The Reno gang robs a train
items.storyFacts: Two masked, armed men robbed the express car of an Ohio & Mississippi train at Seymour, Indiana, taking a small safe. Generally attributed to the Reno brothers, it is considered one of the earliest peacetime robbery of a moving train in the US.
items.hook: Wartime train robbery by guerrillas and deserters had been common. This was one of the earliest as ordinary crime.
items.displayName: The Reno gang robs a train

items.title: The Granite Railway opens
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest railroad in Massachusetts opened, hauling stone from a Quincy quarry toward the Neponset River for the Bunker Hill monument. Loaded cars descended by gravity under rope and winch; empties returned by animal power.
items.hook: America's first commercial railroad hauled the stone for a monument to the Revolution.

items.title: Rogers, Ketchum & Grosvenor ships first locomotive
items.storyFacts: The locomotive builder Rogers, Ketchum & Grosvenor ships its first locomotive, the 4-2-0 Sandusky, to an Ohio railroad.
items.hook: Locomotive manufacturing was becoming a specialized American industry.
items.displayName: Rogers, Ketchum & Grosvenor ships first locomotive

items.title: Los Angeles reaches the sea
items.storyFacts: The newly assembled locomotive Los Angelos marked the opening of the Los Angeles & San Pedro Railroad with free trips between the city and Wilmington on San Pedro Bay. It was one of the earliest railroad in southern California.
items.hook: Before the harbor, before the boom  -  a 21-mile line to the water.

items.title: Grand Trunk links Montreal and Toronto
items.storyFacts: The Grand Trunk Railway completed its line between Montreal and Toronto.
items.hook: The spine of central Canada, finished a decade before Confederation.
items.displayName: Grand Trunk links Montreal and Toronto

items.title: The Denver & Rio Grande
items.storyFacts: William J. Palmer organized the Denver & Rio Grande to build a narrow gauge railroad from Denver to Mexico City.
items.hook: It never reached Mexico City. It did produce the most spectacular mountain railroading in North America.

items.title: One of the earliest documented sleeping car service
items.storyFacts: Service began on the Philadelphia, Wilmington & Baltimore. An advertisement in the Baltimore Chronicle announced cars for night traveling with berths for twenty-four persons each, used for one of the earliest time that night.
items.hook: An earlier February 1838 service on the Cumberland Valley may have beaten it  -  but this one is documented.
items.displayName: The first documented sleeping car service

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Michigan
items.storyFacts: The animal-powered Erie & Kalamazoo opened between Port Lawrence, now Toledo, Ohio, and Adrian in Michigan Territory. It received its first steam locomotive in January 1837.
items.hook: It opened before Michigan was a state.

items.title: Theodore Judah dies
items.storyFacts: Judah died in a New York City hotel of yellow fever contracted crossing the Isthmus of Panama. His wife accompanied his body to Massachusetts for burial.
items.hook: The engineer who made the transcontinental possible died six years before it was finished, killed by the isthmus route he was trying to replace. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Eugene Debs is born
items.storyFacts: Born in Terre Haute, Indiana.
items.hook: Fireman, union founder, Pullman strike leader, five-time presidential candidate  -  one of whose campaigns he ran from prison.

items.title: The Verdi robbery
items.storyFacts: Six armed robbers took $40,000 from the express car of a Central Pacific train at Verdi, Nevada. A second robbery 24 hours later and 400 miles east netted a similar amount.
items.hook: Two big robberies on the same railroad in two days.

items.title: Central Pacific reaches Oakland
items.storyFacts: The Central Pacific completes its line from Sacramento to Oakland, California.
items.hook: This gave the transcontinental system a direct rail connection to San Francisco Bay.

items.title: One of the earliest passengers killed in America
items.storyFacts: Two died in a derailment caused by an overheated axle on the Camden & Amboy at Hightstown, New Jersey. Former president John Quincy Adams escaped injury; Cornelius Vanderbilt suffered broken ribs and a punctured lung.
items.hook: A former president and the future king of American transport, in the same wreck. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.
items.displayName: The first passengers killed in America

items.title: John Bull, assembled by a man who had never seen one
items.storyFacts: New Jersey legislators rode behind the Camden & Amboy's new locomotive Stevens on a short track at Bordentown. Built in England by Robert Stephenson & Company, it was assembled in America by mechanic Isaac Dripps, who had never before seen a locomotive.
items.hook: It arrived in crates with no instructions. It survives today in the Smithsonian.
items.displayName: John Bull, assembled by a man who had never seen one

items.title: Horse-drawn rail service reaches Manhattan
items.storyFacts: Horse-drawn passenger service begins on the New York & Harlem along the Bowery in Manhattan.
items.hook: Before steam dominated city railways, horses pulled scheduled rail cars through New York streets.

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in Cuba
items.storyFacts: The Guines Railroad opened between Havana and Bejucal. Cuba became the seventh country in the world with an operating railroad.
items.hook: Cuba had a railroad before Spain did.

items.title: Farmers versus the Michigan Central
items.storyFacts: Arson destroyed the Michigan Central freight house at Detroit, the worst incident in a wave of vandalism. Farmers angered by inadequate compensation for livestock killed by trains had been opening switches, obstructing track, and shooting at trains. Twelve were convicted of sabotage and arson in September 1851; twenty were acquitted.
items.hook: William H. Seward defended the accused ringleader. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Old Ironsides
items.storyFacts: Matthias Baldwin's locomotive Old Ironsides was tested on the Philadelphia, Germantown & Norristown, running about six miles and reaching 28 mph. It strongly resembled the imported John Bull, which Baldwin had examined during its assembly.
items.hook: Baldwin looked at a British engine, went home, and founded what became largest then known locomotive works in the world.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1832. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: The founding of American civil engineering
items.storyFacts: The American Society of Civil Engineers and Architects was founded in New York City. Architects was later dropped from the title.
items.hook: The profession organized itself because railroads demanded it.
items.displayName: The founding of American civil engineering

items.title: Grading begins at Omaha
items.storyFacts: Grading for the Union Pacific began at Omaha, Nebraska, after Lincoln's November proclamation set the eastern starting point there.
items.hook: Track-laying did not actually begin until July 1865  -  the war came first.

items.title: Locomotive engineers' insurance association forms
items.storyFacts: The Locomotive Engineers' Mutual Life Insurance Association is established in Port Jervis, New York.
items.hook: Railroad brotherhoods increasingly provided members with financial protection as well as workplace representation.

items.title: Steam service begins in Charleston
items.storyFacts: The South Carolina Canal & Rail Road operates its locomotive with cotton and passenger cars in Charleston.
items.hook: The railway was among the earliest in the world to use steam locomotives in regular service.

items.title: Pennsylvania Railroad begins through passenger service
items.storyFacts: The Pennsylvania Railroad begins passenger service between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh without a change of cars.
items.hook: Through service was an important step toward seamless long-distance travel.
items.displayName: Pennsylvania Railroad begins through passenger service

items.title: Vanderbilt takes the New York Central
items.storyFacts: Cornelius Vanderbilt was elected president of the New York Central and allowed to select the board of directors.
items.hook: He got there by refusing to interchange traffic at Albany in January, stranding the Central's passengers in the snow.
items.displayName: Vanderbilt takes the New York Central

items.title: The Victoria Bridge
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest train crossed the St. Lawrence on the 10,284-foot Victoria Bridge. Designed by Robert Stephenson, the single-track structure was fully enclosed and tubular, with smoke ventilation problems not unlike a tunnel's.
items.hook: A two-mile iron tube over a river. Passengers hated the smoke.

items.title: Nova Scotia's first railway section
items.storyFacts: The Province of Nova Scotia completed one of the earliest section of the Nova Scotia Railway between Richmond, in Halifax, and Truro.
items.hook: A government-owned railway from the start  -  a Canadian pattern.

items.title: One of the earliest president to ride a train
items.storyFacts: Former president John Quincy Adams rode the Baltimore & Ohio between Baltimore and Relay House, Maryland, in a carriage loaded aboard a flat car.
items.hook: He rode in his own carriage, strapped to a flatcar. First president to travel by rail  -  though out of office.
items.displayName: The first president to ride a train

items.title: South Carolina Canal & Rail Road is organized
items.storyFacts: The South Carolina Canal & Rail Road Company is organized in Charleston, setting up one of the earliest American steam-railroad ventures.
items.hook: The company would soon become central to the transition from canals to steam railroading.
items.displayName: South Carolina Canal & Rail Road is organized

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in New Jersey
items.storyFacts: Fourteen miles of the Camden & Amboy opened between Bordentown and Hightstown. The locomotive Stevens, also called John Bull, was among those placed in regular service.
items.hook: Within a year it produced America's first passenger fatalities. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.
items.displayName: The first railroad in New Jersey

items.title: One of the earliest railroad in New Hampshire
items.storyFacts: The Nashua & Lowell opened between Nashua, New Hampshire and Lowell, Massachusetts.
items.hook: New England's mill towns strung together by rail.
items.displayName: The first railroad in New Hampshire

items.title: One of the earliest railroad west of the Mississippi
items.storyFacts: An inaugural train ran over the Pacific Railroad of Missouri, five miles between St. Louis and Chelteham  -  one of the earliest railroad in Missouri and one of the earliest to operate west of the Mississippi River.
items.hook: Five miles. The transcontinental was ten years away.
items.displayName: The first railroad west of the Mississippi

items.title: The B&O reaches the Ohio
items.storyFacts: The Baltimore & Ohio reached the Ohio River at Wheeling, Virginia. One of the earliest train from Baltimore arrived on January 1.
items.hook: Twenty-four years from one of the earliest spade to the river it was named for.

items.title: Christmas Day in Charleston
items.storyFacts: The Best Friend of Charleston made its formal public debut, running numerous trips for the citizens of Charleston on the South Carolina Canal & Rail Road.
items.hook: America's first scheduled steam railroad service began as a Christmas outing.

items.title: First train enters Chicago Union Stock Yard
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest train enters Chicago's new Union Stock Yard.
items.hook: Chicago's stockyards would become one of largest then known rail-served meatpacking centers in the world.
items.displayName: First train enters Chicago Union Stock Yard
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1865. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: The Knights of Labor
items.storyFacts: Garment cutters in Philadelphia organized the Noble Order of the Knights of Labor.
items.hook: It would go on to lead some of largest then known railroad strikes in American history.
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1869. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: One of the earliest American iron rails
items.storyFacts: One of the earliest iron rails made in the US were rolled at Mount Savage, Maryland. The 500 tons produced during 1844 were U-section, weighing 42 pounds to the yard.
items.hook: Until then, American railroads imported their rail from Britain.

items.title: Beating the deadline by minutes
items.storyFacts: Henry Farnham's Mississippi & Missouri Railroad reached Iowa City just minutes before a midnight deadline, claiming a $50,000 reward offered by the city.
items.hook: Cities paid bounties to be reached. This one was collected with minutes to spare. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: One of the earliest railway tunnel in Canada
items.storyFacts: The Brockville & Ottawa Railway opened its tunnel at Brockville, Ontario.
items.hook: It was abandoned for decades and reopened as a walking tunnel with light installations.
items.displayName: The first railway tunnel in Canada

items.title: Gotthard Base Tunnel
items.storyFacts: 57.1 km, twin single-track bores, up to 2,300 m of rock overhead, 28.2 million tonnes excavated, 17 years, CHF 12.2bn.
items.hook: It is a base tunnel: rather than climb the Alps, it goes through their feet on an almost level grade, so freight no longer needs banking locomotives. Rock temperatures near 46C and the squeezing Tavetsch massif at Sedrun were the hard parts  -  ground that flows under pressure rather than holding a shape.

items.title: Seikan Tunnel
items.storyFacts: 53.85 km, of which about 23 km lie under the Tsugaru Strait; roughly 240 m below sea level.
items.hook: Driven through fractured volcanic seabed with major floods during construction. It was begun because ferries across the strait kept sinking in typhoons.
items.source: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time
sources: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time

items.title: Channel Tunnel
items.storyFacts: 50.5 km, about 38 km undersea; three bores  -  two running tunnels and a service tunnel.
items.hook: Boring machines from both coasts met mid-Channel within centimetres, using a chalk marl layer identified as the one stratum soft enough to cut and tight enough to stay dry.
items.source: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time
sources: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time

items.title: Qinghai-Tibet Railway (Golmud-Lhasa)
items.storyFacts: 1,142 km in the second phase; about 960 km above 4,000 m; highest then known point Tanggula Pass at 5,072 m; Tanggula station at 5,068 m is the world's highest then known.
items.hook: The real enemy was not altitude but permafrost  -  ground that thaws under a warm embankment and swallows the track. Engineers used elevated viaducts, crushed-rock cooling embankments and thermosiphons to pull heat out of the soil. Coaches are oxygen-enriched.
items.source: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time
sources: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 2006. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Ferrocarril Central Andino
items.storyFacts: Reaches roughly 4,780 m at Galera; dozens of switchbacks, tunnels and bridges out of Lima.
items.hook: Engineer Ernest Malinowski climbed a near-vertical Andean wall using zig-zag switchbacks where no curve could fit. For nearly a century it was highest then known standard-gauge railway on earth.
items.source: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time
sources: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time
items.supersededNote: Superlative bounded to 1908. Re-check before airing; records move.

items.title: Nilgiri Mountain Railway
items.storyFacts: 46 km metre gauge, climbing about 1,900 m on grades up to 1 in 12.5 using the Abt rack system.
items.hook: Still worked by steam. The rack pinion engages a toothed rail so the train climbs by gearing rather than friction  -  the answer to a grade no adhesion locomotive could hold.
items.source: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time
sources: Show research file; verify superlatives at script time

items.title: Rhaetian Railway Albula / Bernina lines
items.storyFacts: Roughly 60 km with 55 tunnels and 196 bridges; the Bernina reaches 2,253 m without rack assistance.
items.hook: The Albula's spiral tunnels gain height by corkscrewing inside the mountain, letting the line climb steeply while the track itself stays gentle. A UNESCO World Heritage site.

items.title: The Westinghouse automatic air brake
items.storyFacts: Patented 5 March 1872, US patent 124,405. Each car carries its own air reservoir and a triple valve. The brake pipe stays pressurised at about 70 psi; a DROP in pressure applies the brakes. Westinghouse's earlier 1869 patent, US 88,929, was the straight air brake, which sent air to apply and was NOT fail-safe.
items.hook: The inversion is the invention. The 1869 brake failed dead if a hose burst. The 1872 design made loss of pressure the trigger, so a parted coupling brakes the runaway half automatically. Failure became the thing that stops the train. Sources disagree on the exact number, and that uncertainty is part of the story.

items.title: Janney's knuckle coupler patent
items.storyFacts: US Patent 138,405, granted 29 April 1873 to Eli H. Janney for an automatic car coupler. Janney had an earlier coupler patent in 1868; this is the second, and the one the knuckle design descends from.
items.hook: A former Confederate quartermaster, working as a dry-goods clerk, designed a coupler that let cars connect without a worker stepping between them. It replaced the link-and-pin coupler that had been costing brakemen fingers, hands, and lives for decades.
